title: A Calendar Invitation Is Still an Untrusted Message
summary: Google’s new blocking option is a useful reminder to verify unexpected calendar invitations before trusting their links, files, or instructions.
body: On August 18, Google announced a new way to block organizers who repeatedly send unwanted Google Calendar invitations. Blocking a Google account now removes the current event, prevents future invitations from that organizer, and adds the person to the account-wide blocklist used by supported Google services. The feature is rolling out gradually to Google Workspace and personal accounts, and there is no administrator switch for it.

The useful lesson is larger than one Calendar button: an event invitation is still a message from another person. A meeting title, video link, attached agenda, phone number, or urgent instruction can look more authoritative once it appears on a calendar, but its placement does not prove that the organizer is legitimate. An unexpected appointment deserves the same pause you would give an unexpected email.

That matters for small organizations because calendars often sit beside email, customer records, and daily operating schedules. A convincing invitation can create pressure to open a document, join a call, change a payment, or sign in through a link. The safe response is not to distrust every new customer or vendor. It is to verify unusual requests through a channel you already know before acting on them.

A concrete action for today is to review how invitations reach your calendar. In Google Calendar on a computer, open Settings, then Event settings, then Add invitations to my calendar. Google offers three choices: add invitations from everyone, add them only when the sender is known, or add them after you respond by email. Choose the setting that fits how your organization schedules work, understanding that a stricter option may require a little more manual review.

Give employees a simple rule for unexpected events: do not use the invitation itself to verify the invitation. Confirm the organizer through a saved phone number, a known email thread, or the organization’s published contact information. If the event is clearly unsolicited, report it as spam. Google’s new blocking option is intended for repeated invitations from Google accounts; non-Google senders are handled through Gmail blocking instead.

Blocking is useful, but it is not a complete cleanup tool. Google notes that blocking an organizer does not remove calendar access you previously shared with that person, and it does not stop every possible Gmail notification tied to an older event. Review calendar sharing separately if the sender ever had legitimate access, and check old invitations manually when necessary.

There is no need to turn calendars into locked-down systems that frustrate ordinary scheduling. The proportionate approach is to control which invitations appear automatically, verify unusual requests outside the event, and know how to report or block persistent spam. A few clear habits keep the calendar useful without treating every square on the screen as trusted by default.
